bullets: Integration undoes differentiation - but what does an antiderivative have to do with area under a curve?
slides.heading: A-Math integration: area, accumulation and the +C trap
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we learn that integration is accumulated area, how Riemann sums of thin rectangles converge on the exact area, how to evaluate a definite integral, and the trap of dropping the +C.

bullets: Explain the antiderivative as accumulated area and the definite integral as the limit of a Riemann sum
Evaluate a definite integral by antidifferentiating, substituting the bounds and subtracting, and never drop the +C in an indefinite integral
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the +C trap.

bullets: A rectangle has an easy area, but the region under a curve has a sloping top
If the top keeps curving, how can we ever get the exact area?
slides.heading: How much area sits under a curve?
slides.notes: Sketch a curve over an interval and ask: rectangles are easy, but this top slopes - so how could the exact area ever be pinned down? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because thin rectangles closing in are the answer.

bullets: The antiderivative F of f is a function with F'(x) = f(x): integration undoes differentiation
The definite integral from a to b is the exact accumulated area under the curve between the bounds
An indefinite integral has no bounds, so it names a whole family of antiderivatives differing by a constant C
slides.heading: Integration is accumulation
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: integration is accumulation - area piling up as x sweeps right - and antidifferentiation is the tool that computes it exactly.

bullets: As x sweeps right, area strips pile up under the curve behind the sweep dot
The antiderivative at each x is exactly that accumulated area, so integrating undoes differentiating
slides.heading: The antiderivative is accumulated area
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch the sweep dot travel right and the shaded strips grow behind it. The height of accumulation at each point is the antiderivative building up.

bullets: Chop the region into rectangles and add their areas: a Riemann sum is an estimate
Make the rectangles thinner and more numerous and the total closes in on the exact shaded area - the definite integral
slides.heading: Riemann sum: thin rectangles converge on the area
slides.notes: Count the wide rectangles first: a rough total. Then watch them halve in width and double in number - the gaps and overlaps shrink, and the sum converges on the exact area.

bullets: Integrate 2x from 1 to 2: antidifferentiate to x^2, then evaluate at each bound
Upper bound minus lower bound: 4 - 1 = 3, so the area is 3 square units
slides.heading: Worked: evaluating a definite integral
slides.notes: Work the three moves in order and name each one: antidifferentiate, evaluate at the bounds, subtract. Four minus one is three - no +C here, because the constant cancels between the bounds.

bullets: The trap claim is: The integral of 2x is x^2.
Every vertical shift x^2 + C has the same derivative 2x, so the indefinite integral must keep the +C
slides.heading: Misconception: never drop the +C
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: x^2 alone names only one curve, but x^2 + 5 and x^2 + 7 differentiate to 2x as well. The +C stands for the whole family.

bullets: Step 1: antidifferentiate 2x to x^2
Step 2: evaluate at the bounds and subtract: at x = 2, x^2 = 4; at x = 1, x^2 = 1; 4 - 1 = 3 square units
slides.heading: Worked example: evaluate the definite integral
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each one as you write it; say: antidifferentiate first, then let the bounds do the work - upper minus lower, in that order.

bullets: Find the indefinite integral of 2x, and evaluate the definite integral of 2x from 0 to 3
Careful - a classmate claims: The integral of 2x is x^2. Explain to them what is missing and why it matters
slides.heading: Your turn: integrate, then evaluate
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call two pairs: listen for the trap - The integral of 2x is x^2. The fix is: Never drop the +C: differentiating x^2 + 5 and x^2 + 7 both give 2x.

bullets: On your own: evaluate the definite integral of 2x from 1 to 3
Watch out for the trap one last time: The integral of 2x is x^2. Say what the complete indefinite integral of 2x must include
slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
slides.notes: Close by reminding the class of the trap - The integral of 2x is x^2. - and the fix: Never drop the +C: differentiating x^2 + 5 and x^2 + 7 both give 2x. Collect the tickets as they leave and check who still drops the +C.
